utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Lausic, I again would like it remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Kay, are you ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if we could look at another document concerning the appointment of Mr. Orsulic and the rotation of the units in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1134, dated the 29th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm producing this to show you that as it pattern that's repeated. We looked at yesterday the 17th; we're now looking at the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Your Honour knows that we've had these documents in evidence, and I produce them during the cross-examination of Mr. Theunens, the whole range of these documents. I don't propose to go through every one with the witness because it would be to no good effect or economical effect, but I do need to show him that it's a sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you make a representative selection and then we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think you've understand what I've said then, Mr. Lausic, that this is just to show you a further example. There it is, Exhibit D1134. As you can see, it's from Commander Budimir of the 72nd, repeating that same 5th of August order that we looked at yesterday, and the order is framed in very similar form to the previous document with, in paragraph 2, Lieutenant Orsulic selected as the commander. But the officers beneath him are slightly different. Sergeant Podrug is a company NCO, has been added; star Sergeant Brnic is this time the 2nd Platoon commander, instead of the previous order it was a man called Vesevic and the traffic platoon was previously a man called Begovic. It is now Ante Pobric. So the appointments changed that Commander Budimir was making beneath Lieutenant Orsulic, but the rotation of the components of the company remained the same. And if we just turn to page 2 so that can you see it's from Commander Budimir and where it was sent to. Again, that continued for the next period, and we've put in documents up till the end of November concerning this. And having shown you that, we will move from the rotation matter to now the daily reports, and you wanted to see the daily report yesterday for the 19th of August, and we've got that as a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 6924.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is the daily report from the 72nd Battalion duty service. This document is similar to certain ones you've seen previously during your testimony. We can see on the first page there's a crime report. No need to look at the detail of that. If we look at the second page in English, but it's still the first page in the Croatian language, further details of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can now turn the Croatian language one to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Other events are described there, about four reporters being detained, giving their identities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see further details there. And then in the last page, safety of military road traffic, we see the report there. And the issue, just to refresh your memory, if you needed it from yesterday, concerned that report that Lieutenant Orsulic had filed with the military police administration, general military police department, concerning the tour of various people from the Ministry of Defence, and I asked you about that document. It was Exhibit D791. And you wanted to look at the daily report for that day to see if there was any mention of that matter in it, and it appears there is no mention of the tour by the Ministry of Defence members on that day. Is there any further comment that you'd like to add now?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report of the duty service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and not a daily report of the MP company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would we have to look in the daily book of the Knin company to see if it is mentioned in there? Would that be the appropriate step to take?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you find it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just looking at this document, we can note who this daily report is sent to at the foot of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can turn the Croatian language version to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you see to whom this document is sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I now want to turn to 65 ter 5630. The document I've just referred to is part of the Prosecution bar table documents, Your Honour, which is why I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we've got the daily report here, as another example of the 26th of September, 1995, from the duty service of the 72nd, we can see here, of a crime reported in the first part. I'd like us to just look at that because it concerns a Knin military police company patrol, seeing and investigating a crime, and we can see what it concerned without going into the detail, but it's the fact of that happening and involving the Knin company. We can also see a report for that day of violations of the Code of Military Discipline, and that concerned something on that day when a Knin military police company patrol discovered a Croatian military member shooting his rifle into the air in Marsal Tito Street across from the Knin forward command post building. Page 2 in the English, we can see that a soldier was arrested by the local military police who seized his rifle, and he was submitted for criminal processing. We can see the other events that happened on that day. And then if we turn to the end of this document, we can see to whom the document is delivered to; and, in particular, I want you to look at number 3, the Split garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, Your Honour, without going through the 100 or so reports that we've had in evidence and bar table documents, we know that all these reports reflect a similar ending. And of the addressees, it is the Split garrison commander who receives this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the point I want to put to you is this: That if this information and breach of military discipline concerned the Knin military police company who were reporting to General Cermak, or subordinated to General Cermak, he would have received this information. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My order of the 14th of August, in item 14, and that's the order we looked at before, which relates to the implementation of the military police tasks in the areas of responsibility of MP units. Item 14, in the last paragraph, regulates in very precise terms that the military police company in Knin shall be subordinated to the most senior commander of the Croatian army in its area of responsibility, to which it -- to which it shall submit its daily report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, for reference, you are referring to Exhibit D47.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of the exhibit. I'm referring to the order of the chief of the MP administration of the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I say that for the record. So a report of this nature, if the Knin company was reporting to General Cermak, would have been sent to him.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daily report of the military police company in Knin, that is, and not the daily report of the 72nd Military Battalion as a whole. This daily report is sent to the commander of the Split Military District because the 72nd Battalion is stationed in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for rising. But the translation came back in line 8, page 6 as "commander of the Split Military District," and I believe if we could check on what the witness may have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, read a portion of your last answer and see whether it is transcribed and translated with full accuracy. You said: "The daily report of the military police company in Knin, that is, and not the daily report of the 72nd Military Battalion as a whole. This daily report is sent to the commander of," and then you said, "Military District." Which Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I said that this daily report of the 72nd Battalion, as can be seen, is also sent to the commander of the Split garrison, as listed under item 3 from among the addressees. It is sent there because the 72nd Battalion was stationed in Split, and he, as the commander of the Split garrison, received that daily report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, you say it's -- under 2 and 3, it is addressed, among others, to the Split Military District Commander and to the Split garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that is because it's a report of the 72nd Battalion as a whole; whereas, units within that battalion may have reported to others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only added that the daily report of the 72nd Battalion was sent to the commander of the Split garrison, because the 72nd Battalion was headquartered in Split; whereas, it had dislocated companies in Zadar, Sibenik, Sinj, Knin, and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to whom would the daily report of the military police company in Knin have been addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my 14th of August order, it was also sent to the commander of the Knin garrison, as listed in the last paragraph of -- item 12, of my 14th of August order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just go to Exhibit D47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is back to your order, dated the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 12, which is page 3 in the English. Paragraph 12 is there in the Croatian language. Page 4, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's what paragraph 12 says there. "The newly established military police units must be urgently provided with the necessary level of accommodation, logistics support, and documents for operations and training. Members of the military police shall work rotating shifts every 20 days," et cetera. That does not say that they report to the garrison commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mentioned in item 14 of the order, in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not mentioned in paragraph 14 that they report to the garrison commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. To the most senior commander of the Croatian army, in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just recap something here in answer to Judge Orie's question. Judge Orie asked: "And to whom would the daily report of the military police company in Knin have been addressed?" And the answer, interpreted for me, was: "According to my 14th of August order, it was also sent to the commander of the Knin garrison as listed in the last paragraph of item 12 of my 14th of August order."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm allowing it to be translated -- it's not only English language, there are other languages. That is not reference to that the reports would be sent to the Knin garrison commander in paragraph 14. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've been looking at documents at two levels. A level of documents communicated by you down to the battalions; and then documents beneath the battalion commander, down to the companies, which have not been referenced to you but are operating at a level below. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you did not know to whom the Knin company was actually reporting to?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify. Are you saying that I didn't know? Or that I was not aware of the fact to whom the commander of the Knin battalion reported on a daily basis, of a Knin company?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know the identity to whom the Knin company commander was reporting to?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not received daily reports of the Knin company --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because they went to the 72nd headquarters, and the 72nd headquarters combined the daily reports of all the companies and then sent a combined report to the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The summaries of all the most important reports, as I have already explained, containing data either on the victim or the perpetrators or the characteristics of the events. We're talking about summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were questioned by Mr. Foster and Mr. Morris and others from the investigation department of the OTP in May of 2004, the transcript we have says this: "For instance, they covered certain areas. The military police company of the 71st Battalion in Knin was subordinated to the highest officer." It's page 12 in the B/C/S, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 13 in the English. For reference purposes, it's page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the first interview on the Friday. Have you got that now, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't been able to locate that in my binder. Can I please have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure. Is that the binder Mr. Foster gave you on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are documents that I was given on the 17th December, 2008. This is actually the transcript of my interview as a suspect, and also my statement provided as a prospective witness. I don't know whether what you are mentioning now are excerpts from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah, because this is important that you see what was said at the time. It's 65 ter 7036.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May -- sorry. I was wondering if Mr. Kay could provide, in addition to page numbers, line references because I'm having some difficulty finding that particular excerpt that he quoted. And didn't flow if it is my inability to find it on the page, and the line reference would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, page 13 of 58, 4965, and 65 ter -- can we go back a page in the English. Can we go back a page in the Croatian. Next page in the Croatian. Other way, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the English version, wrongly put into your statement is 71st, instead of 72nd. Can you see that? You mentioned the 72nd, but it's wrongly put into the English here for a reasoning with, in fact, connected with Mr. Foster's question. But we can just go through this. "For instance they covered certain areas. The military police company of the 72nd Battalion in Knin was subordinated to the highest officer, commander in its area of its [sic] responsibility, and its area of responsibility, the area of the town of Knin and the surrounding areas, and a platoon in Drnis and the Benkovac platoon. And they deal with it the same way, and they deal with all members in uniform of the Croatian army, whether they deal with them through their own activity or following reports of the civilian police, citizens, et cetera." Mr. Foster said: "So who was the 71st Battalion in Knin subordinated to?" Which we know is an error. And then the next passage is: "First of all, to the commander," the commander of the 72nd Battalion, it should be, "and the commander was subordinated to the commander of the Military District." In English, we have: "All right," which doesn't appear there in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just move it up the page a bit on the English. The other way, sorry, it's my mistake. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We then have: "Horizontally to the highest ranking commander, to the highest ranking commander of the Croatian army in its area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which we can see on the right, that that is part of the combined answer. And then Mr. Foster says: "So in Knin that would be General Cermak, would it?" And then your answer in the Croatian language, perhaps you could just read that out.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, just to illustrate the dimensions of what I'm saying and the problems in our functioning within the cooperation between the Ministry of the Interior and ourselves. On 7 August, I was -- I received a telephone call at 1845 by Mr. Moric, the assistant minister, and he told me that Mr. Smiljan Reljic who was in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you very much. We're looking at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go back, then, if we can just scroll up the B/C/S higher up the page, please, just stop there. And if you could just read out what Mr. Foster said to you in B/C/S at line 9.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Who was the 71st Battalion in Knin subordinated to?" I would like to say that this is completely wrongly defined issue, or question, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just read out your answer beneath that to his wrong question of the 71st Battalion in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that he asked me who the company of the military police of the 72nd Battalion was subordinated to, the one that was stationed in Knin, and my answer to that was the following as under bullet points 11, 12, 13, and 14: "First of all, I meant the company of the MP in Knin was subordinated to its commander, and that was the commander of the 72nd Battalion. And the commander of the 72nd Battalion was subordinated to the commander of the Military District. And in horizontal lines, and, again, I'm talking about the company of the military police in Knin, to the most supreme commander of the Croatian military in their area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the English could be turned to page -- the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just read out in Croatian at line 16 what Mr. Foster said.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In Knin it would be General Cermak, would it not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then your answer at line 18.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yes, that's true." And then a break: "And now to illustrate the dimensions of what I'm talking about and the problems of how we cooperate" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop there. Thank you. You would agree that under the rules, as we discussed yesterday, your Article 9 rule of the military police concerns the highest ranking commander by function?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, that's right. Yeah. That was not a part of your discussions with Mr. Foster, the issue of highest ranking by function. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence this morning, you did not know, and as a matter of fact, to whom the commander of the 7th Company, or the Knin company, was reporting to. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was not, in fact, a question either that Mr. Foster asked you, as to whom the 7th Company in Knin were reporting to. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I wouldn't call it the 7th Company. I would call it the company of the military police in Knin, and as for the rest, I agree. What I'm saying is that this company did not bear a numerical part of its name, either at that time or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to make sure we're clear, then: He did not ask the question of you to whom or whether you knew to whom the Knin company was reporting to in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the transcript, the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He, Mr. Foster, put the name "General Cermak" to you on the issue of the highest ranking commander in the area, but that was a hypothetical issue concerning the command and subordination of the Knin company, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move from there now to another section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you would allow me to ask a few clarifying questions. Mr. Lausic, it is clear you have clearly responded to Mr. Kay's question. You did not know to whom the police, military police company in Knin, was reporting. Now, on the basis of your earlier instructions that reports should be sent to the -- let me -- to the highest ranking commander in the area, could you just list for me to whom you would expect -- under your instructions, to whom you would expect the military police company in Knin would report? Whether they did is another matter but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken, I already said last week that in Knin there was a specific situation which reflected in the following: In Knin there was a forward command post of the Military District with the complete command, irrespective of the fact, where, at any given moment, the commander of the Military District was, the command of the Military District was in Knin. The second specific characteristic was that the forward command post of the 72nd Battalion of the military police was also in Knin. Its main headquarters was in Split. However, since it was active in the area, its command was in Knin at that moment. And there was also the company of the military police, which was newly established and stationed in Knin. Daily reports issued by the 72nd Battalion, or, rather, its duty service as may be seen, was submitted to the command of the Military District Split. It is only to be assumed, and I am just answering your question as to what my assumptions are. It is assumed to that a battalion of the military police -- the company of the military police in Knin did not send reports to the forward command post of the Military District Split, its own daily reports, because the events, pursuant to which the members of the company acted, were dealt with in the daily reports of the 72nd MP Battalion. And these reports were sent to the command of the Military District. It is to be assumed that their daily reports were sent to the most senior officer in their area of responsibility, and that would be the commander of the garrison there, whose name was known and who was appointed as the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second because we are moving from 72nd Battalion to Knin company. We have seen on the documents shown to you by Mr. Kay where you said, These are not reports of the Knin company, that they were sent to the Split -- the Military District command, Split, and to the garrison commander in Split as well. Now, I'd like you to focus on the company only. The company in Knin would -- if they would follow your instructions - if it is part of your instructions; if not, tell us - would report to whom exactly? Who would be on the list of addressees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the 72nd MP Battalion or, rather, its duty service. That is the first step in the vertical ladder, to the commander of the Knin garrison, to the chief of the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mention the commander of the Knin garrison. Is that because you consider him to be the highest ranking military commander in the zone of responsibility? Is that why you include him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they did or not, as you said to Mr. Kay, you do not know; but that is what you expected them to do on the basis of your instructions. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I think the test is actually different; it's highest ranking by function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I said, Because you considered him to be the highest ranking military commander, I meant to -- but let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I withdraw that. If you want to further explore --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to deal with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Because you used the wordings not always with functional. I think a lot of your questions it was, Did I function --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I've taken it from the order, it is without function. If I'm dealing otherwise, it is by function. And on the transcript they didn't use the term -- Your Honour will recollect that the original translation we had in the case was wrong, and that phrase "by function" was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I was referring to just the text of item 14. If you want to further explore the matter, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Knin, the highest ranking military commander by function in the zone of responsibility is not the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also true. But I stressed the specific situation in Knin as a provisional location where the forward command post of the Military District was stationed; that's to say, the command of the Military District. We also have the forward command post of the 72nd Battalion stationed there. We also have the command of the commander of the Military District, and we have commanders of certain units stationed in Knin. Which units exactly, with which commanders bearing which ranks, I don't know. However, the logic I'm following, the reasoning, is that the commander of the company in Knin whose activities are already covered in the daily report sent to the commander of the Military District, as we were able to see, his own daily report relating to his company would be sent to the levels that I mentioned in answer to His Honour's question; namely, the commander of the 72nd Battalion -- or, rather, its duty service, the commander of the garrison, the chief of the police station in Knin, and probably some other levels within the company itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So to make it clear, then, that's on a theoretical level. You are saying that was an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not speaking of the theory. I'm telling you what my reasoning, my logic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we just look at a document that may be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is an exhibit, D996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 16th of February, 1995. It's from the garrison commander in Split. And it's addressed to the chief of General Staff, General Bobetko, and it concerns the functioning of the Split garrison. Have you ever seen this document before, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It will be important for you to have an opportunity to read it. We have seen this already in court. And if you read the first page -- tell us when you have read the first page, then we'll change over.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the English, please. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document was sent just to General Bobetko, Chief of Staff, from Colonel Zoricic of the Split garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go back to the first page, because it's often difficult to take in all information quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was February 1995, and it was critical of the establishment of the Split garrison as you can see. And saying that there were problems, and we can see the terms of the letter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we now turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of the problems that he refers to, as we see in the second paragraph, is the authority of the garrison commander, garrison control officer, and garrison duty officer. "I have no authority over military police, and I do not even cooperate with them, since the garrison institution has been ignored by the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander. Without the assistance and possibility of using military police, it is impossible to reach the required level of order and discipline." And we see other complaints and then his proposals. And in proposal 3: "The garrison commander shall be given authority and one military police company in the city of Split area shall be subordinated to him." Firstly, did General Bobetko ever refer this problem to you?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember this particular problem. I am familiar with Colonel Zoricic, and I know that there were problems between him personally and the commander of the 72nd Battalion. The way the information was conveyed to me, he was known to send requests to the military police for matters that went beyond the scope of their activity. As for Colonel Zoricic, the order from the minister of defence and the chief of the Main Staff, General Bobetko, of the 27th August 1993, had in its enclosures the instructions regulating issues from the purview of garrisons where, in item 4, it is referred to the engagement of military police units in very precise terms. And it is regulated in what way in cooperation with the military police was supposed to be established. The commander of the 72nd Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will turn to those now because we have them as an exhibit. Exhibit D34. Sorry to interrupt, but I think it may assist the Court to know what the witness is referring to. This is it Exhibit D34, organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison HQs and is the reference cited by the garrison commander in Split in his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us last week that you received this first on the 25th of January with the documents that Mr. Foster gave you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that the first time you had seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain about it. I may have received it for my information back then, although it's not stated here, but I saw it the other day for the first time in the documentation that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. If we just look at this carefully because it concerns the setting up of the garrisons as we see in the headnote. And the order to set up a comprehensive system of command, cooperation, and coordination at the level of garrison headquarters. We can see paragraph 1 there. But it's paragraph 2 that I'd like you to look at carefully. And it says this: "The garrison headquarters [sic] commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units, except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order, and discipline at the garrison headquarters outside of barracks and other military facilities within the tasks provided by the rules of service of the armed forces." Now, do you note that there, that it says the garrison headquarters commands don't have an operational function? Did you know that before, that that was one of the orders concerning the garrisons?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in such precise terms, but I did know what the tasks of garrison commanders were in accordance with the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The tasks were set out in the 1992 rules of service, and we will go back to look at them. But this was the order, wouldn't you agree, as to how the garrisons had to function?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the rules of service don't make that fact about the garrisons not having an operational function. It is not said in those terms in the rules of service; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lawyers should be better placed than me to make a proper interpretation of the document; they drafted it. My interpretation would not have legal validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm stating a fact because we've looked at it, and it's often helpful to do that so that we have a base for the next question, if you understand. Now, in the orders that you issued and we looked at yesterday, most specifically the one on the 14th of August that refers to operational commands, Exhibit D47, daily operational commands, do you see that there is a problem between the orders issued by the military police and this function of the garrison here as set out in the 1993 order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is there. However, I have to say that the rules governing the organisation and work of the military police as bylaws - in other words, regulations inferior to legislation which serve as provisions implementing legislation, in this case, the Law on Defence - is a piece of regulation of an earlier date and, therefore, takes supremacy in relation to operational orders. Another thing is that the rules governing the organisation and work of the military police were passed in 1994 and antedates the 1993 order by date as well. In those rules, in Article 9, that is, daily operational command is mentioned on the part of the most senior commander by function, commander of the Croatian army, and let me be quite precise --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could read it -- read it out again because it's the word "regular" that is it used, rather than "operational" in Article 9. If you read it out, Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 9 of the rules governing the organisation and work of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia reads: "The rules were adopted in February 1994 as bylaws. In performing regular military police tasks, the military police units shall be subordinated to the commander of the Military District, commander of the Croatian navy, commander of the Croatian air force..." That's just -- or, rather, "to the most senior commander of the Croatian army by function in the area where the military police units operate or are active." Let me just add the following. My interpretation of the rules as a piece of bylaws which has supremacy over the order, also in terms of dates -- or, rather, not my interpretation, but a proper interpretation of the rules should be given by the lawyers. This is my position in relation to that on the basis of my legal knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, for the record, it was Exhibit P880 the witness was referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just looking at paragraph 2 here, we've looked at the non-operational function. But it says the garrison headquarters commands don't have the right to issue orders to Croatian army units except precisely prescribed authorities regarding, work, order, and discipline at the garrison headquarters. So, again, a -- were you not aware of that fact in 1995 and when you were interviewed in 2004 about the --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the order or the 1993 instructions. I gave my statement on the basis of the rules governing the organisation and work of the military police and the orders which were issued pursuant to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. When you were interviewed and your statement taken by Mr. Foster, Mr. Casey, Mr. Morris, and others, you had your documents that you had issued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly are you referring to when you say "your documents"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The military police administration documents that you issued at this time as the chief.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The ones that I obtained from the archive when I was preparing for the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were not asked to review other documents that we have looked at in the course of your cross-examination. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can look at number 4, because you referred to point 4, that refers to the commanders of Military District and other commanders "shall study the enclosed directive in a" -- I know you also were referring to number 4 of the instructions. But ... we will look at that; don't worry. This is an important --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an important -- number 4 as well. And to be fair to you, have you had the time to absorb all these -- all the detail in this document?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what period do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, have you had time to look at this document carefully until I've started asking questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just summarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, as we saw. Paragraph 4 here requires those commanders to study the directive, and based on specific circumstances, set out concrete tasks for garrison headquarters regarding work, order, and discipline and implementation of the prescribed tasks. Were you aware that the garrisons were going through a process of organisation and change in order for them to function properly?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge of the workings of the garrisons was quite superficial, save for Colonel Zoricic as the commander of the Split garrison. I don't recall any other garrison commanders at this time, I must admit. I remember him by - and this is only to put it mildly - some of the peculiarities of his work mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just so that we finish this page, just looking at number 5, that there was a requirement that their work be monitored and assessed to ensure that the situation encountered was taking all the necessary measures for work, order, and discipline at the garrison to the required level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see the time, and we're turning no the next section of this as I said we would, as the next phase of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll already ask Mr. Lausic to leave the courtroom. Mr. Lausic, we'll have a break, and then I'll further inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, your estimate was one day. You started yesterday in the second session of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm on the last lap, and I think I would be finished within the next session, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which makes it one and one third of a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that during the break. We will have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed. Leave is granted for the additional time you asked for. However, if you would not use all of it, that would certainly be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour, and I will bear that in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we were looking at these organisational orders regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison headquarters, Exhibit D34. And just to remind you, before the break, we looked at the fact that this was setting up the garrisons' tasks that had to be done in advance and review of the work that was being done. Shall we go now to the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English. And it's instructions on regulating some issues within the jurisdiction of garrison headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see in 1 that duties and tasks for garrison headquarters that are outside their original garrison headquarters due to temporary occupation of their territory, that they are able to perform at their current locations, prepare documents. Can we just look at one issue here, which may be an important issue for you to consider. Until the 5th of August, of course, there was no garrison in Knin. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you an answer because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This instruction here requires tasks to be devised to set up garrisons that are outside the place where they have been designated. If we go to number 4 here, which is the one you wanted to look at. It's the next page, and it's called "employing military police units." And it says: "The ZM commander is required to arrange a procedure with the closest unit of the military police of calling MP units and having them intervene in the case of unrest, accidents, et cetera, when an MP unit is indispensable to establish order and discipline in the area of the garrison..." headquarters. What I want to put to you is this, that that is a written procedure as to how the garrison should operate with the military police if there is trouble in the garrison area which would be a written protocol of how to respond to trouble. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I'm reading number 4 here, I can say that what you have just put to me may be seen as arising from the contents of number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next matter, next sentence we should look at is: "Also arrange for temporary employment of MP patrols to supervise work, discipline, and conduct of military personnel in public places." Just looking at that, that required the garrison commander to use temporary military police patrols to supervise what would be the rules of the garrison as to how people should behave in relation to their military conduct. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This may be understood from bullet point 4, and it may be said that what you have just put to me is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is because the garrisons were a place that the military based itself, and there was a required level of behaviour of how the military should behave in that area to enable it to be part of the town or community. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the Croatian army were duty-bound to comply with all the rules that regulated the work in their units, discipline, the discharge of certain duties, a whole host of regulations applied which are contained in the collection of rules and regulations which were applicable to the Croatian army at the time. I'm talking about the general rules of service in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go now to page 7 of the English, and it's paragraph 17, which I think is on the next page in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, no, page after that in the Croatian language, please. If it can go -- if we can look at the top of the page in the Croatian and go back a page in the Croatian to the bottom of the page. Sorry about that. It's -- ah, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Lausic, point 17?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. And you looked at that with Mr. Tieger. And it's headed "regulating order, discipline and supervision of the conduct of military police." And the garrison commander should lay down instructions on order, discipline, and supervision of the conduct. And we can see it's uniform schedule of working hours, time of exchange of internal service organs, conducting of military personnel in public places, type of supervision, restricted locations, use of public transport. Again, this refers to regulations as to how people should behave in the area so that good order and discipline is maintained by military personnel. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I'm reading this text, I can say that what you just stated is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what we've been looking at in relation to the garrison orders and rules and instructions are all matters that would be relevant to a stable and peacetime situation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to give a precise answer to your question because in 1991 or therefrom, we were in war. And the specific characteristics of the Croatian theatre of war was reflected in the fact that over 1000 kilometres of the front line, in its entire length almost, went along the urban settlements and settled areas or, rather, along their borders, or even intersected those urban areas like in Vinkovci, Gospic, Zadar, Karlovac, Sisak, and so on and so forth. And the characteristics of towns in the Republic of Croatia where the units of the Croatian army were deployed was the fact that they were all very close to the front line, so we cannot talk about a peacetime or areas that were not affected by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Taking Knin in August to November 1995, the circumstances in Knin at that time were not a normal set of circumstances. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. After having been liberated, immediately thereafter, Knin was a town to which refugees were returning. They would come to visit their destroyed houses. Many of them had been mobilized into the units of the Croatian army. They wore Croatian army uniforms. Many wore Croatian army uniforms, although officially they did not belong to the ranks of the Croatian army. One would say that this was a neuralgic location from the point of view of safety of all aspects, if we're talking about security of an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now go to Exhibit D32, which is the service regulations you referred to in 1992. And they were the ones produced by Mr. Foster in the interview. Page 11 in the English, and we're looking at paragraph 50 onwards, under the heading: "Garrison." I believe we've got a copy there, Mr. Lausic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I do have the document in handwritten version. I took this document immediately before I came to this Tribunal to provide my testimony as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's page 17 in the Croatian version. We've got that there. Shall we have a look at this because it's referred to you -- in your statement. We see number 50 about the garrison. And then number 52: "The garrison commander is responsible for placement, order, discipline, and service in the garrison. All units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, discipline, and service." Now, the order we've been looking at from 1993 of organisation and work in the garrison expresses the role of the garrison commander differently, don't you agree? Exhibit D34, when we've looked at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I would like to emphasise once again, in order to be able to provide a precise answer -- answers, you will have to consult legal experts. I am providing my answers based on my own knowledge and familiarity with the law and on my experience. So my opinion should not be taken as an opinion of a legal expert who would be able to give you a proper implementation of these regulations and bylaws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand that, and the point I want to make to you is that how these rules concerning the garrison were developed were such that they took the form of the rules within that order that we looked at earlier in 1993. And the power of the garrison commander over units and institutions within the garrison concerned those rules that he had to draft and prescribe, setting out how people should behave within the garrison. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only agree that this was to be found in the 1993 order, as one of the items of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking instructions, Your Honour, from my colleagues on matters that need to be covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, in relation to that. In your statement, you said that General Cermak, if he saw a crime, would have a responsibility to report it to the Military District Commander. Do you recollect that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you quoted the transcript correctly, whether you quoted my words from the transcript correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And what I wanted to put to you is this: That General Cermak could also refer that -- refer a matter, if he had seen a crime, to the military police. That would be an appropriate way of him referring something that had gone on, that was a crime, to refer it to the military police. That would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obligation to report crimes is something that every citizen of Croatia has according to penal code. So it doesn't apply only to members of the Croatian army. Pursuant to the penal code of the Republic of Croatia, every citizen is duty-bound to report a crime of which they learn and which are prosecuted, ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that could be carried out in the same way by any staff of General Cermak also reporting the matter on, so that if there had been a crime brought to his attention and then a subordinate of his or an officer working with him reported it to the military police or the civil police, that that would be a correct way of proceeding. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He did not have a duty as a garrison commander to investigate a crime.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? You mean crime investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If a subordinate of his committed a crime, he had a duty to deal with the act of his subordinate. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But he was not under any obligation to carry out a proper crime investigation. He only had to -- reported his suspicion that somebody was involved in the commission of a crime, and then the investigation is carried out by -- either by military police, or civil police if the suspect is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And looking, as we have, at those documents today, it is right, is it not, that they do not establish that the military police company in Knin was under the day-to-day command of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it in my document of the 14th of August, my order issued to the company commander to subordinate him to the highest commander there. And by that order, I give the company commander instruction to report to that person, to the highest commander, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And one other matter I want to deal with: General Cermak phoned you on one occasion whilst he was in Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I stated that there was one telephone conversation in relation to securing a warehouse or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did General Cermak, in fact, in that conversation that he had with you ask you to send more military police to the region to help keeping the law and order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such a conversation taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it correct, though, that in fact further reinforcements of military police were sent to Knin to supplement the troops of the 72nd Battalion from other battalions of the military police in other parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that yesterday, where, in addition to the members of the 73rd Battalion who had been at the disposal of the 72nd Battalion as reinforcements from day one, I also sent the armoured vehicles with crews from the 67th, in order to reinforce the company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the battalion's numerical designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We looked at that yesterday. It was from the 66th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. I've finished my questions now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic, will be it you or Mr. Kuzmanovic who cross-examines Mr. Lausic? Mr. Lausic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the start of my examination, I should like to refer to your answer of last week when Mr. Misetic asked you about the state policy in relation to the overall events related to Operation Storm. Your answer can be found in the transcript at page 15596, line 16, where you answered in the following way: You said that the state policy was reflected in the order which you received as early as at the first meeting which was held on the 2nd of August in the war room. The meeting with Mr. Susak in the preparatory stage of Operation Storm was the occasion when the minister said that the military police had to be energetic in its activities and its preventative efforts. You also said that the state policy was also reflected in the efforts you made, you, as the most senior representative an officer of the military police, as well as the Ministry of Interior, which could be seen in numerous documents. Mr. Lausic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am at page 15596 and don't see that reference. Perhaps that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [In English] Line 16. It is an answer in my -- state policy was reflected in the order which I received as early -- at first meeting on the 2nd of August in the war room. So maybe I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mikulicic please speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, would you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to arrange this, Your Honour. Or maybe I should use another microphone. Like this, is it better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The interpreters are thanking you. But please turn-off the microphone to the right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So should I repeat what I said. I was referring to the transcript on the page 15596, line 16th. And where the answer of Mr. Lausic begins with, "in my view, the state policy," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone else has this opened. I have a printed version of the transcripts, and at 15596 that's not the reference. I can try turning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is a transcript from 30 of January. Well, I will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page you are referring to, 15596, is on the 2nd of February. So there we have already a small problem. You have -- apparently, you are quoting. Now our search engines allow us to search for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's page 15512, beginning at line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. My mistake. I apologise. I'm not good with the figures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the right-hand microphone of Mr. Mikulicic please be turned off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're requested to switch off at least the right-hand microphone, but I don't see that -- I don't see that it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Only the left one is switched on, Your Honour, on my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If everyone else switches off all the microphones, we'll see what happens when just the left one is open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I just turned on my -- I turn-off my left microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to a lot noise when that microphone is open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, it goes beyond my technical experience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't rely too much on mine. Could you perhaps use the other microphone for a second and see whether the sound is any better. So switch off the left one and use the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think all the -- do you call that rumble, or ... that disappears. So perhaps if you could rearrange your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Finish with all technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lausic, regardless of the technical difficulties we have experienced in the meantime, do you recall this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I confirm it fully. This was in answer to the question of what I understood as the state policy, which is something I referred to at a meeting with my commanders, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I did not tell you this at the start. Since we both speak the same language, we should be mindful of the fact that we have to make a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can do their job.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you were a high-ranking official in the military police. You were the chief of the military police administration. However, you held another important function, and that was that you were the chief of security for the president of the Republic, unofficially since 1991 when you were summoned, and officially as of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to correct you. I became chief of security for the president of the Republic in January 1991 as a member of the Ministry of Interior, since, at that time, the Croatian army was not yet in existence. It was only on the 1st of December, 1991, that I was appointed by the president of the Republic to the newly established military police administration within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia pursuant to an oral decision of the president of the Republic, and a written decision on appointment to that particular position was given to me in February 1992, if I'm not mistaken. However -- however, let me note that as the chief of the military police administration, I remained, until the death of the president, a member of the security staff of the office for national security, and, as such, I was involved in the application of security measures for the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this precise answer, Mr. Lausic. In fact, it was my intention to ask you this: In that capacity you held, you were oftentimes in a position to be in the presence of the highest ranking representatives of both the civilian and military authorities in Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, Mr. Lausic, on such occasions, and I mean you personally, receive an order, either formally or informally, that the citizens of Serb ethnicity in the Republic of Croatia should be mistreated, harassed, that crime at their expense should be tolerated, that arson or theft should be tolerated or even encouraged with a view to causing their departure from the Republic of Croatia -- or, rather, with a view to driving them out of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my answer, I will be focussing on two individuals only, namely the president of the Republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the Minister of Defence, Mr. Gojko Susak. Throughout the time, including the period when I was the chief of security for the president of the Republic, in the course of 1991 through to the time when Minister Susak died in 1998 and when President Tudjman died in 1999, I had never received from these two individuals an order or anything else in any other form to the effect that I would be asked to do something contrary to my notions of work ethic, my world view, my professionalism, as an individual who, 20 years previously, was always a man representing the law. Quite the contrary. In every occasion where I spoke to Minister Susak and referred to such conduct of members of the Croatian army as was -- as constituted misconduct or even criminal conduct, Minister Susak's reaction to such reports on my part was vehement. He asked that the police take energetic action in investigations, that it cooperate closely with the Ministry of the Interior. He asked that every incident of opportunist behaviour be reported him, be it that on the part of the Croatian army officers or on the part of the colleagues from the Ministry of the Interior, and there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Madam Registrar to pull up 65 ter 1838, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lausic, you've just mentioned Minister Susak and his attitude towards this issue. On the screen in front you, you can see an order issued by Defence Minister Gojko Susak on 25th September, 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"]. In this order under 1, Minister Susak orders the military police administration to urgently take all necessary operative action to discover the perpetrators in the ranks of the HV of any criminal offences which may have been committed during the execution of set tasks in the Gospic area in September 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"]. Would this order, as a matter of fact, be a reflection of the minister's position, with regard to the issues that you have just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example in a written form. He issued a written order to take all operative action necessary. However, those who knew Minister Susak also knew that he was not a man of many words but that his facial expression told it all. He was not a man who would cover -- try to cover his actions up with written orders. His oral order accompanied by his facial expressions, which left no doubt in anybody's mind as to what he was thinking at that moment when he was issuing his orders, meant a lot more than any written order at moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhibit which was MFI'd as P2164, but I would like to tender it into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I have no objection. I'm not just sure if there is any particular extraneous reason for the MFI. Assuming there wasn't, then I don't have any objections; that is, it may have been MFIed in the normal course of business or they may have a particular reason I'm not aware of at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should check that as well. But at least if this exhibit marked for identification, if we have to decide on admission, there is no objection on your side, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the contrary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the contrary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, page 41, line 12, it should be 1993, September 1993. I think there is another reference to 1992 as well, earlier in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the document was certainly 25th of September, 1993, yes. That's then corrected. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lausic, you have just said that when talking about the prevention of all forms of illegal action, you held, before Operation Storm and after Operation Storm, meetings with the representatives of the Ministry of the Interior. Would that be a correct answer?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I assumed the duties as the chief of the military police administration, as one of my fundamental duties that I imposed upon myself and upon my associates was close cooperation with the Ministry of Interior, and I did that for three fundamental reasons. It was a fact that in 1992 and thereafter, there was some antagonism between members of the Ministry of the Interior and members of the Croatian army. What I'm saying is that the first ones who joined the defence of the state in 1991 were members of the Ministry of Interior. They were the only armed establishments in Croatia at that time. And then the Ministry of the Interior issued an order in 1992, and pursuant to that order, members of the civil police changed combat and camouflage uniforms and put on their blue uniforms and went back to their fundamental peacing activities and maintenance of law and order. At the same time only members of the special police of the Ministry of the Interior remained engaged in combat. This was the origin of antagonism between members of the Croatian army and members of the civil police. My first task, therefore, was to try and curb any expressions of antagonism through the joint work of the military police and the civil police. The aim was to influence members of the military police, and I have already said that the professionalism of the members of the military police was at a very low level at that time. Their equipment level was at an even lower -- even lower level, so that the cooperation was supposed to deal with both antagonism and lead to the process of direct education of members of the military police. And also it went a long way in providing assistance in specialist equipment, especially for the crime prevention police. And in that joint action, we were stronger in dealing with some incidents and situations that, in some cases, were even seen to be very dramatic. So what I can say is that cooperation with the Ministry of Interior was, from day one, a must in my work, and it was my pleasure to able to establish that cooperation at my levels of communication and that I met with support and assistance. And I have in mind two assistant ministers of the interior, one of them was the assistant for general police, Mr. Moric; and the assistant for crime police, Mr. Benko, with whom I had already cooperated or, rather, I started my police career with the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Lausic. When you were talking about these meetings and preparations, they started even before Operation Storm was launched. I'm referring to number 173 in your witness statement of 2003. You said there that on the 3rd of August, on the eve of the launching of Operation Storm, a meeting was held at the Ministry of the Interior and the following persons attended, and then you go on to list all of them. And that the main subject of that meeting was cooperation in the engagement of military and civil police in the events that would ensue thereafter. Is that correct, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would now ask you, since we have seen a number of documents throughout your testimony and the testimony much of some other persons in this courtroom, that there were a lot of efforts invested into ensuring law and order in the newly liberated territories after Operation Storm. However, there also a lot of problems with the implementation of those ideas and efforts on the ground. You yourself mentioned some of those problems that you were faced with in the implementation of your ideas. First of all, it was a large and relatively inaccessible terrain. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I'm not mistaken, over 7.000 square kilometres of the newly liberated area infested with mines and other explosives, not very well accessible and riddled with hundreds of other bigger and smaller problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but I would also like to say that a major problem for the newly established civil authorities in the area was the fact that that area had been under occupation for four years outside of the system of the regular civilian powers, and I'm referring here to the Ministry of Interior. Is that correct, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've also said just a minute ago that that there was another situation regarding the numbers, and I'm not talking about absolute figures but also in relative terms, that there was not enough educated police officers. In that case you cooperated with the Ministry of Interior, especially with the crime prevention police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we embarked on the process of educating officers and non-commissioned officers of crime prevention police, and you know that this happened only in the second half of 1992, when, from the Ministry of the Interior, a person who joined the administration, was Mr. Ante Gugic, Assistant Minister for crime police department, and he was the one who embarked on a mission to educate policemen and to equip them. However, before that, as soon as he assumed -- as soon as I assumed the duty, I held a meeting with the chief of the police academy of the Ministry of Interior, Mr. Josko Arnovic [phoen], and we agreed at that meeting that he would organise courses and the courses would be held at the police academy for future members of the civil police and that I would ask him to give me an allotment of places on those courses and I would send my men, members of the military police, to such courses, and they would learn about policing at that those courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Lausic, and objectively, there was a lack of policemen, and they were not well-educated, and this was a fact. However, the situation got better gradually.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did get better gradually. We had a higher number of policemen who had received formal education at higher schools of education and universities, and also, the level of professional policing became higher. In the second half of 1992, I established an educational centre of the military police which exists to this very day as part of the military police regiment. This institution applied different models of training, in order to provide students with different police work specialties and subspecialties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam Registrar to show us D567, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on what you were just saying, Mr. Lausic, I will show you a document bearing your signature of the 16th of September, 1995. This is an analysis of the use of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia in Operation Storm. I don't think I have to ask you if you're familiar with the document since you're its author.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us quickly go through the document, in view of the positions you expressed. Let's look at page 2 of the document, second paragraph. Which says that the anti-terrorist units of the military police were being prepared through training for attacks and mop-up operations from the remaining groups, individuals, and firing points. Mr. Lausic, we discussed military police units at great length, and I would kindly ask you to describe the tasks of military police units in a few words.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
