utterances.text: I will try to put it as succinctly as possible. Now what were the causes and purposes of setting up anti-terrorist units within the MP units? In August of 1992, on the order of the chief of the Main Staff, General Bobetko, and with the approval of the minister of defence, the joint forces of the military police were engaged in combat aimed at liberating the hinterland of Dubrovnik. Unfortunately, I had members of the military police wounded or killed in the course of these activities. I made an analysis of the action that was carried out, and at the level of the ministry -- of the military police administration, we concluded that it was not appropriate or advisable to deploy the military policemen who carried out their regular military police tasks to combat activities because of the inferior level of their training and expertise required for the conduct of what are purely combat activities. As a follow-up, in June 1993, we carried out a selection with the consent of the minister of defence of members of the military policemen and set up anti-terrorist units of the military police. Their tasks consisted solely of the following two: Dealing with difficult situations as authorised officials of the military police, and by that time, we had been faced with hostage situations within the Croatian army, and with very difficult incidents involving the use of arms, explosives. The second task was combat, should the military police be issued with such an order. Their level was going up throughout the time, and I have the pleasure of telling you that many of their members who are still active can be found in the missions in Afghanistan and in other places where the Croatian army is sent for missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Lausic, as a policeman of many years, you must be familiar with the structure of the Ministry of the Interior, and you must, therefore, be familiar with the role of the special police within the Ministry of the Interior. And correct me if I'm wrong: Would it be fair to say that the combat unit of the anti-terrorist military police units was a match for the special units of the Ministry of the Interior, in terms of the tasks given to them, the level of training, and the circumstances and tasks to be carried out by these units?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that fully, and I can tell you that there was always this sort of healthy competitive relationship and a certain degree of envy vis-a-vis the members of the special police whom we regarded as brothers in arms, though brothers who were better armed and better trained than we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what sort of uniform members of the anti-terrorist unit of the military police wore?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uniforms changed, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm specifically referring to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it in general terms. The uniform consisted of green overalls, green fatigues, combat fatigues, which came complete with what we referred to as "the green gear," unlike other members of the police who carried what we referred to as "the white gear." Members of the anti-terrorist units had that particular green gear. However, I do allow for the possibility - and this was something that I was able to observe on the ground - that some of the members of these units also wore the combat camouflage uniform. And almost as a rule, they would have over their green fatigues a camouflage vest. However, the clothing differed, and what I referred to is only, generally speaking, what can be described as the uniform of the anti-terrorist units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In view of what you have just said, and I suppose you know what sort of uniforms special police forces of the Ministry of Interior wore, is it possible to say that a person who is not privy to these details might mistake members of these two particular sets of units. That's to say, to mistake special units for anti-terrorist units and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the special police units had black berets with two insignia: One was a rounded emblem of the military police, and the other emblem which was that of the anti-terrorist police, which was a stylised image of a falcon within a coat of arms. The same sort of insignia was sewn onto the left sleeve of the fatigues; whereas there was the standard patch of the members of the military police of the Croatian army on the right sleeve.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter misspoke. The description refers to the anti-terrorist units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The special police members had the patch which consisted of three intersecting lightening bolts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lausic, my questions arose from your testimony -- or, rather, the testimony in general that we were able to hear in the courtroom so far, where international UN monitors and other witnesses had different views on the topic. Let me, therefore, ask you the following: In your testimony so far, you spoke of Major Juric as one of the officers who was supposed to serve as your eyes and ears, as you put it, to be acquainted with the situation on the ground. It is true, is it not, that Major Juric was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time he held the position of chief of one of the departments of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Major Juric have any sort of powers in relation to members of the special police of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me present to you the testimony of Mr. Philip Berikoff who testified on the 1st of September, 2008, in this courtroom, which at page 7602, line 23, where he said that, in his view still today, the special police was involved in some operations around Kistanje, because on numerous occasions I, personally, met up with Major Ivan Juric from the military police. On numerous occasions, he wore the grey uniform of the special police, which led me to assume that Major Juric also controlled a number of various police units, as well as the forces of the special police. In fact, him wearing that grey uniform led me to assume that there must have been a presence of the special police in the area as well. How would you comment on these assumptions by Mr. Berikoff and there view of your earlier answers?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely incorrect that Major Juric should have any sort of powers over members of the special police. Even the grey colour of his uniform is something that was never seen in the Croatian army. It never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the document we have on our screens, which is the analysis of the use of the military police. Let us focus on the statistics contained therein, specifically at page 8 of the Croatian version. This is the ERN number 413. There it is stated that the military crime police in cooperation with the crime police of the Ministry of Interior carried out criminal investigations in respect of 321 criminal offences. Next, the numbers of murders and deaths and arsons and mining and other criminal offences are listed. It is also stated that out of the known perpetrators, 79 were members of the Croatian army, whereas 274 were civilians. At page 9, the document lists the measures that were taken, in order to raise the general level of security. I will not be going into details in that regard. Is this not in fact an indicator of the efforts made by the military police in this narrow area pursuant to the order of Minister Susak dating back to 3rd August, 1995, which was still at the preparatory stage for Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to answer this in a single sentence that I am known to say when some of my acquaintances or friends ask me about how my case, in relation The Hague Tribunal, would end, and they have been asking me that ever since 2004. My answer consists of one sentence only. All my professional and intellectual efforts -- I invested all my professional and intellectual efforts in order to -- to take all that to my first subordinate levels, in order to make sure that it is conveyed down to the last military policeman, so that, together with the colleagues from the Ministry of Interior, and this is something that could be seen from a number of documents which I issued as orders, the orders could be used to change the methods and tactics of action in order to reinforce certain areas whilst highlighting the need for energetic action. And I don't think a policeman need be told twice what energetic means, zero tolerance. And another must was the cooperation with the colleagues from the Ministry of Interior in order to prevent to the greatest possible extent and ultimately to investigate and process all the threats to the security of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia. Now, how efficient were we? Well, given the resources we had, given the level of training and education we had achieved by that time, given the problems faced -- given the problems that the mobilised policemen faced who could not be demobilized because of their social welfare since it was the only means of their subsistence, given the civilian authority which was unable to become fully operational in the newly liberated area, and given hundreds of other problems. But nobody can deny one thing, and this is why, when I was answering a question by His Honour the Presiding Judge, I said that my testimony, regardless of the form it may have or the capacity in which I give it as a suspect, a witness, or subsequently perhaps even in the capacity of an accused, that my testimony would always be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic. So can we with agree, then, can't we, that you, as the head of the military police and as we go even lower towards the lower echelon, you did your best to prevent any crimes and illegal actions. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am a bit hurt when I heard a sarcastic remark by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let's leave this to the end. You will be given an opportunity by the president of the Trial Chamber to say a few words. But let's focus on what I'm trying to achieve here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Yes, Mr. Mikulicic, we'll have a break now. I noted that questions easily take two minutes or more, whereas answers of five minutes are not uncommon. That is not the most efficient way of cross-examining a witness and to get focussed answers on matters you'd like to bring to the attention of the Chamber, could you please keep that in mind, if we resume after the break. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly address the parties on the following matter. The reasons why we're not sitting in this case on Thursday and Friday do not exist anymore. Now, the Chamber is fully aware that since this was announced well in advance that many people might have made arrangements which make them unavailable. Nevertheless, the Chamber -- we have the same problems among the Judges. Nevertheless, the Chamber would like to be informed whether it is totally impossible to sit on Thursday or Friday or whether there are any possibilities still left, because there are courtrooms, there are -- I'm -- we don't have to -- we don't need to hear your answer immediately. If you would send an e-mail to Mr. Nilsson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just briefly tell that you Mr. Kehoe and I, in fact, do have other plans related to this case for Thursday and Friday, and we will not be in The Hague at that point. But it is my understanding in communication from Mr. Hedaraly yesterday -- I don't know if I can say this publicly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you were going to say, so you have rely upon your own conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding because of witness scheduling issues, let me put it that way, we will not be sitting on Monday and Tuesday of next week, and, therefore, it may be an opportunity concerning tomorrow's witness to push him back to Monday and Tuesday if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in conjunction with that because that issue tomorrow is one that we have been addressing. We have filed one motion, and we are filing another motion concerning the exhibits because it relates back to the appellate chamber decision that needs to be reconciled before we move ahead. Because, frankly, Your Honour, I know we have not addressed that because there hasn't been time, but I would say well over -- approximately three quarters of those exhibits bear on that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of the -- of course, the Chamber is working on it as well. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what your position is, but it seems that the Gotovina Defence is not available, both counsel and co-counsel are not there, so that makes it impossible, of course, no one can be blamed for making his plans if it is it announced that we will not sit. That seems to be an obstacle which is impossible or almost impossible - we do not know yet - to surmount. But, the parties, if they could sit together and see what could be done as far as Monday and Tuesday is concerned, that, of course, will be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The parties have been in contact, Your Honour. I'm, of course, not sure what can be done beyond what has been communicated to the Court, but obviously we'll do our best to stay -- to do what can be done under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that knowledge, of course, might also give some flexibility and avoid that witnesses are coming and have to wait for three or four days before -- perhaps a small portion of their testimony is still to be given then and perhaps to postpone arrival. But I have got no idea about the practical arrangements made for the witnesses to come, so I leave it entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And to the extent it is helpful, we'll try to keep the Senior Legal Officer advised and work toward whatever arrangements can be made. Because of the status of the case, the opportunities for adjustment are more limited and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to continue? The Chamber has in mind -- I don't know whether you said you needed one session. You've taken approximately a half. There is also request to deal with scheduling issues to make oral submissions on that. I don't know how much time will you need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be precise, I will need that in that circumstances for finishing my cross, not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Mr. Tieger, could you tell us how much time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm estimating 15 to 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That brings oral submissions on scheduling in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I might be less, but I understand the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lausic, let's dwell upon this topic that we've already started discussing, and that was the issue of you having encountered situations among the top echelons of the Croatian government that illegal conduct would be favoured, and you provided an extensive answer. To follow up on that, did you ever notice that at the lower operative levels, there were some attempts of the sort, i.e., were there cases when illegal actions were not punished? Was there some of an agreement to that effect among the lower level of command of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try and be succinct in answering your question, but I believe that I have already answered your question in my testimony so far. I believe that at the lower command levels in the Croatian army, and when I say that, I mean primarily non-commissioned officers and lower-ranking officers, there was a rather tolerant attitude towards a lack of discipline among the troops. However, this tolerant attitude did not arise from -- and I'm convinced that did not arise from any orders, but, rather, that as individuals, they hailed from the same body of people over whom they were in command at that moment, and against the principles of professionalism, they instilled emotions into their decision-making process. They did that to empathize in a way with perpetrators of illegal actions as people who could not avoid the traps of their own frustrations, the traps of their own emotions as those who had suffered in the war and who had been persecuted during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer, Mr. Lausic, and now I would like to move on to another very brief topic, and this is the position of the special police in the events. I have looked at numerous reports of the military police, numerous analyses. Correct me if I'm wrong, I have never encountered any information pointing to the fact that members of the special police of the Ministry of the Interior were considered either responsible or caught red-handed in the commission of crimes. Do you have any different information than the information that I gained by looking at the documentation available to me?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything that would jog my memory about an event that was dealt with by the crime police about any incidents which involved members of the special police of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lausic. Just a few questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was some discussion earlier today, and perhaps, if I recall correctly in earlier sessions, concerning the language of Article 9 and the question of most senior HV commander versus highest HV commander by function. So I wanted to ask you if you could explain to the Court what the difference is between the most senior HV commander in an area of responsibility and the highest HV commander by function, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer will be my opinion. As for the correct interpretation, you would have to talk to legal experts. In all the militaries of the world, including the Croatian army, the rank worn by a person, the patch representing that rank that they wear on their shoulders -- or let me put it this way. A star more does not necessarily mean that that person can be in command of one star less or lower down the chain. There are situations when an officer with a lower rank is appointed to a higher position than another officer with a higher rank. By virtue of that, the duty that that person discharges implies that that person is the highest ranking officer in a unit or in an area of responsibility. Sometimes it goes by rank, and sometimes it goes by the function that a person holds. But, as I say, as for the proper interpretation, you would have to consult experts. This is my interpretation, and I base my explanation on the situations that I encountered in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to some questions that you were asked last Thursday, the 29th, and this is at about page 15391, in that area. You were asked questions about the section for prevention of general offences, whether or not the head of that section was subordinated to the chief of crime investigation, and then whether or not the chief of crime investigation was subordinated to you. And then you were asked whether the same organisational structure existed within the battalions themselves; that is, whether, within battalions there was a chief of crime investigation and a separate crime investigation section and separate sections. At that time you indicated you wanted to see the establishment manual of a battalion which was contained in the systemisation document, in order to be precise about structure and numbers and so forth. I'm not going ask you for precise details that might require the manual, but I want to ask you some general questions concerning that issue. First of all, you have explained at length, or discussed at length, Articles 8 and 9 and explained the nature of subordination of the military police battalions to the commanders of districts pursuant to Article 9, and I wanted to ask you whether or not that included all members of the military police within those battalions, including crime investigation police.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. A battalion in all of its segments, i.e., in all of its specialities and subspecialities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could quickly call up 65 ter 706.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a document dated the 22nd of September, 1995, from the department of the crime investigation military police, signed by chief major Milas and sent to the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Colonel Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Was this part of the bar table submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Has been disclosed to us Something you were going to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, no, I don't believe it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm, again, not going be able to re-cross given that I have had no notice that this exhibit was going to be used. And in order to be able to put things back in the proper context as the Court might have noted from my cross-examination, I need some time to prepare documents. I would object to the fact that even in e-mail, there has been no disclosure that there was an intent to use this document in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I could -- one of two choices: I could withdraw the document; we could bar table it later. I thought it would be helpful in this context to raise it, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I would prefer that because then it will give me an opportunity to bar table our documents, but I won't get the opportunity if he puts it to the witness to put mine to the witness, and so I would prefer it be bar-tabled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I have not. So I would have to look through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be wise to just -- not to say that the Chamber will close its eyes, but that you at least read for a second what is there and whether it causes you the problems you expect they will cause you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The issue is, I can read the document, but I don't know what the question is going to be, and so I wanted to object before we get into questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I -- I do understand that. Of course, the Chamber would prefer -- I mean, bar table documents are not the preferred way of receiving evidence. That's the reason why I'm asking you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but I would take a look right now, but I will also note it that -- obviously, I don't think I need to state that it's not preferred to not disclose -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... reason for the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know when it came up. Of course, I have not seen the document either. Mr. Tieger, if -- of course, another way of dealing with the matter is that you -- that you phrase the question you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then not to ask the witness at this moment to answer the question so that Mr. Misetic is informed to the fullest possible -- and then we will hear whether he still objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I do understand, Your Honour, and if I were Mr. Misetic, I probably would have made the same objection, so I understand what the point is. So let me -- I can either phrase the question now in general to the Court or put to the witness. I don't care either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you tell Mr. Misetic here, open in court, what question you would like to put to the witness in relation to this document, then the Chamber will -- earlier said, well, the Chamber will close its eyes, now, it will certainly not close its ears at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Basically whether or not this document is a example or reflection of the fact that the crime investigation police were part of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we'll stipulate to that, so there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's done. Then please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you also discussed earlier in your testimony at 15253 the fact that military police battalion commanders and company commanders had to report to Military District Commanders on tasks and activities. And a similar question, did those tasks and activities about the battalions and in this case the 72nd Battalion include the tasks and activities of the criminal investigation police within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to object. If we could just in the question -- what reports are we specifically talking about? I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there any way you could include this in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me read specifically from the excerpt to which I referred earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 15253, the following question was asked and answered. "Question: Were the Military District -- military police battalion commanders and the company commanders supposed to provide the Military District Commanders with information about their execution of military police tasks pursuant to Article 10? "Answer: Absolutely so. They had to report on all of their activities; that is to say, within each reporting period, they had to report on everything they had done." And my question, Mr. President, and, Mr. Lausic, in particular, was whether or not that answer included also the tasks and activities of the criminal investigation police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my objection is that that excerpt comes from Mr. Tieger's direct examination, so it is not something that arose in cross. The second issue is if he could, again, be more precise in terms of what specifically, when he says "report," what reports are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... My first objection would be that it's not -- if it's not something that arose out of cross but out of his direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me clarify that, Your Honour. I indicated the nature of the issue that arose in cross. I simply turned to that earlier excerpt from direct in order to focus the question and hopefully to expedite it. It does not seem to have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may put the question to the witness. You are invited to specify your question in relations to the reports, and I noticed that on line 9 and on line 10, I find "[Overlapping speakers] ..." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my apologies for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, again, I have directed your attention to the question of reports. Can you tell us, please, to what extent the Military District Commanders were to be advised of the tasks and activities of the criminal investigation police, within that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to daily reporting -- or, rather, daily reports - and we have seen some examples here - different groups of tasks and duties carried out over the past 24 hours are mentioned. Firstly, under the title: "Crime," that paragraph deals with the events that had to do with the commission of various crimes, as well as the investigations which had either been launched or had already been completed. So this paragraph or the first part of every report speaks about the activities of crime police within the military police unit, as well as of the activities of the crime police over the past 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the interests of time, Mr. Lausic, I want to move to an issue that was raised on Friday, when questions were asked about what a military commander was required to do in the face of information about criminal activity or other forms of misconduct by his troops. And I believe you explained -- and that can be found at -- in the -- I don't know if it was beginning at, or that was the heart of that discussion. But at or near 15533, I think you explained what would have to be done and what actions -- and that such actions had to be taken without awaiting the end of court proceedings for that particular offence. This was an exchange during which you and Mr. Misetic explicitly disagreed. He brought your attention to Article 15 of the rules on organisation and work of the military police. Then you explained that the disciplinary proceedings are always conducted by the commander, either through a disciplinary investigation at the end of which, if a minor breach of discipline -- disciplinary measures -- disciplinary measures imposed or where a major breach of discipline is involved, then there are disciplinary charges brought. You continued -- I think that's at 15536. And then at 15538 you indicated that if there are reasons to suspect there were breaches of discipline or rules of service, that is an obligation on to itself for the commander to initiate disciplinary proceedings, as well irrespective of what kind of information he received from the military police. And then there's a discussion in that case about a specific case. Any that, I think, was the nature of the discussion, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- do you remember the discussion -- Mr. Misetic, I see that -- Do you remember the discussion? Well, it was not a discussion. It was question and answers on what still had a memory military commander had to do. If you have that clearly in your memory, then we can perhaps do without a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. And if I could call up P1007 quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking to be brought up on the screen, Mr. Lausic, the Code of Military Discipline. I just wanted to bring your attention quickly to a couple of provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just put on the record, and it may assist Mr. Tieger in terms of what I understand our discussion was about. And Mr. Tieger said it was about criminal activities, and, in fact, the discussion, and I think the witness will confirm, was about disciplinary infractions that may have led to the criminal activities, and that and that the commanders duty concerning the disciplinary violations that may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now Mr. Tieger was stopped in summarising. Let's then -- I said we can perhaps do without summary, and the witness, in an earlier answer, seemed even to be able to repeat a question almost literally that was put to him one of the previous days, so, therefore, at this moment, unless any other indication will appear, the Chamber understands that the witness remembers that series of questions and answers. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to bring your attention quickly to three provisions within the Code. First Article 19, which is found at page 7 of the English, and I ... Article 19, Mr. Lausic, if you -- it's on the screen. I'll just read the first part: "Superior officers shall decide the disciplinary responsibility of their subordinates in accordance with prescribed procedure and shall hand down disciplinary measures as authorised by this Code." If we could turn quickly to Article 22: "The commander of a brigade or corps or more senior commanders shall be empowered to pronounce all disciplinary measures prescribed under this Code." And then quickly to Article 61, if we may. And Article 61 states: "On learning of a disciplinary violation by a subordinate, the superior officer in the position of company commander, a corresponding position or higher, must immediately take all necessary measures to collect relevant evidence and inform his superior officer." Mr. Lausic, my question was simply whether or not those provisions were -- are consistent with the explanation you were providing about the role and responsibilities of a commander who learns about acts of misconduct, including crimes.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my answer is fully consistent with the Articles you've just presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could turn quickly to 65 ter 5670.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I could just inquire again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, 65 ter 5670 is a document dated the 8th of September, 1995. It's issued and signed by General Gotovina. And it is an order putting in force listed measures against all perpetrators who forcefully seized flats and refused to move out, indicating that the 4th Guards Brigade commanding officer shall impose disciplinary measures under his authority and that the 72nd Military Police Battalion commanding officer shall file criminal charges through his specialist staff to the military prosecutor's office in Split. The distribution on this was to the 4th Guards Brigade, the 72nd Military Police Battalion. And, Mr. Lausic, is this consistent with your understanding of the powers of a Military District Commander in the face of information concerning misconduct or criminal events?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it is already in evidence, and it was extensively discussed through the witness Botteri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is it no need to tender it. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's correct. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber has no questions for you at this moment, but I think I promised you to give you an opportunity to add anything you considered -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Shall I recross after he finishes or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind. I hadn't forgotten. Yes. I thought would make more sense once he had added anything. So if there's anything you would like to add. You say, That's important; we missed it. You should now then have an opportunity to do so. This is not an invitation for long speeches but just to bring to our attention what you consider really necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In my answers to the questions put to me by Mr. Mikulicic, I said what I meant to say in my final word, in fact. Throughout my career, especially throughout the career during which I was the chief of the MP administration, which in fact lasted for 12 years, five years of working on the development of the military police, and eight years of my efforts to try and raise that particular element of the armed forces to a higher level, I can only say that, at the end of that military career, during which I held the same position was a time during which the military police as the first armed force to take part in the IFOR operation in Afghanistan, where it is still present alongside NATO members for which participation, it was highly commended. These men, who are now [Realtime transcript read in error "These men, who are not to be found..."] to be found in Afghanistan, were the same individuals who had to be made soldiers between 1991 and 1995. They had to be trained as soldiers and had to advance their knowledge and specialties they had after the war. I am quite proud of that, and I believe that all these documents clearly show what sort of efforts I invested into that process. Thank you very much. There's nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The transcript, page 70, line 3, the witness said that "all those men are now to be found in Afghanistan," not "are not to be found."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it. That you say that they are serving in Afghanistan. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Briefly if we could return to P1007, Madam Registrar. Further cross-examination by Mr. Misetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5 in the B/C/S and page 10 in the English, please. I'm interested in Article 31 which I think is at the top in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you can start to read that. Mr. Tieger showed you a few Articles of the Code of Military Discipline. I'd like to show you Article 31, and ask you to read that. It says: "In situations where the authorised officer finds that the offence against military discipline is also a criminal offence, the case should [sic] be sent via regular channels to the authorised prosecutor. If he thinks that it is in the interests of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary proceedings [sic]." Is that consistent with your understanding of the rights and duties of a commander in the event that a -- what could be characterized as a disciplinary offence is also characterized as a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to distinguish between the crimes upon which the crime police acts as the primary service to react to one's report of a crime in order to ascertain the existence of the grounds for suspicion that a crime was committed and informs the commander of that particular event. Article 31 states that the duty to file a criminal report is one of every officer of the Croatian army, where he makes an assessment to the effect that a crime was indeed committed. He forwards the case to the military prosecutor. The military prosecutor, as you most certainly know, under the Croatian legislation, can forward the case that he received from an officer of the Croatian army to the military police in order to carry out preliminary proceedings with the aim of establishing certain facts. Once they establish the facts, the case is returned to the military prosecutor to make subsequent decisions. So we have the criminal offences that the military crime police will process, and we have crimes which are initiated by the officer of a given unit of the Croatian army through his lawyer and sent to the -- further on to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Quickly, if we could go back to 65 ter 5670, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown this order. In the preamble, General Gotovina refers to the fact that he is issuing this order based on an order that he, himself, has received from General Cervenko. Do you have any knowledge of what General Cervenko had ordered in his order to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with this order. However, the problem of forced entry into apartments was a problem that was present always in the Croatian army, and we reported on that problem to the highest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally in terms of the work of the crime police, I think we went through this at some length about OA Varivode, but the day-to-day investigations being conducted by the crime police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, the status of ongoing investigations, et cetera, would be reported to Mr. Budimir but would also go up the vertical line to the crime police section in the military police administration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can give you a precise answer. In other words, I don't fully understand the question. Do you mean to say that the military crime police sections attached to battalions are, in professional terms, vertically subordinated to the military crime police department of the MP administration? Yes, of course. Similarly, other specialties and subspecialties have that subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question is they would -- in addition to the fact they were subordinated, they would also send written reports to the vertical line in the administration, pursuant to the fact that they were subordinated professionally to them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not professionally subordinated. You have to distinguish the professional vertical line of subordination. The crime -- the military crime police section of the 72nd Battalion and the chief of that section is always subordinated to the commander of the 72nd Battalion, according to all the different aspects from his purview. However, the professional vertical line, through which he seeks advice, consultations, or suggestions is the chief of the department of the military crime police within the MP administration. And only he, as an expert, can provide him with an answer of this professional nature. The commander of the 72nd Battalion is not a crime expert, and can he only get that sort of expertise through that professional vertical line of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. To be very precise, though, would the crime police head in the section of the 72nd send reports to the crime police chief in the MP administration in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would probably do that through the commander of the 72nd Battalion to me, as the chief of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony. I have one question for you, Mr. Mikulicic. You put to the witness the order dated the 25th of September, 1993. Are you going to submit the -- present to this Chamber the response as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me, Your Honour. I just forgot this. I would like to tender it into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was, whether you were also going to present to us the response that came because there was a time-limit set, seven days from the 25th of September, 1993, whether we get a report with a long list of all the crimes discovered and investigated, or whether it was just a response saying nothing happened. Do you have the response? Could bar table it, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe this is also a part of the OTP bar table, Your Honour, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That was not on my mind. Thank you very much. Mr. Lausic, the parties, a little bit less, the Chamber, has kept you busy for quite some days. I would like to thank you very much for coming and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties, and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.
